Indiana's data center footprint, as captured here, is small and mixed in character: six listed facilities, a reported total capacity of zero megawatts, and entries that include a university GIS learning resource alongside commercial and institutional operators.

The commercial and institutional facilities, DartPoints in Columbus, Digital Crossroad in Hammond, and the Indiana University Data Center in Bloomington, represent the clearest cases of purpose-built infrastructure. The Amazon AWS facility in St. Joseph County is the one hyperscale-adjacent name in the set. The remaining two entries in Tippecanoe County, one labeled Agricultural and Biological Engineering and one labeled Learning GIS, do not read as data center facilities in the conventional sense, which raises questions about the completeness and consistency of the underlying source data.

The zero-megawatt total is the most significant caveat. It means the power dimension of this state's compute infrastructure, the figure most directly relevant to understanding AI capacity and grid load, is absent. Without megawatt figures, it is not possible to say anything about Indiana's role in the broader compute supply chain or its grid exposure. What the data establishes is geography and operator identity for a handful of sites, and nothing more than that.
